title_en: Hangzhou Zhuomuniao Shoes v. Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce of the People's Republic of China and Qihao (Group) Co., Ltd. — administrative dispute over trademark
ruling_gist_en: According to the provisions of Article 40, paragraph 1 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China, a registered trademark that violates the provisions of Articles 10, 11, or 12 of that Law, or that was obtained by fraudulent means or other improper means, shall be cancelled by the Trademark Office; other entities or individuals may request the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board to rule on the cancellation of the registered trademark. The term 'improper means' in the above provisions refers to means other than fraudulent means that disrupt the order of trademark registration, harm the public interest, improperly occupy public resources, or seek illegitimate benefits in other ways. Where a registered trademark only infringes specific civil rights and interests, the above provisions shall not apply, and the matter shall be examined in accordance with Article 41, paragraphs 2 and 3 of that Law and other corresponding provisions.

full_text_en:
Hangzhou Woodpecker Shoes Co., Ltd. v. Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce of the People's Republic of China and Qihao (Group) Co., Ltd. — Dispute over Trademark Dispute Administrative Case

【Ruling Summary】

Pursuant to the provisions of Article 40, Paragraph 1 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China, if a registered trademark violates the provisions of Articles 10, 11, or 12 of that Law, or was obtained by fraudulent means or other improper means, the Trademark Office shall cancel the registered trademark; any other entity or individual may request the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board to rule on the cancellation of the registered trademark. The term "improper means" in the above provision refers to means other than fraudulent means that disrupt the order of trademark registration, harm public interests, improperly occupy public resources, or seek illegitimate interests by other means. If a registered trademark only harms specific civil rights and interests, the above provision shall not apply, and review shall be conducted in accordance with Article 41, Paragraphs 2 and 3 of that Law and other corresponding provisions.

When hearing trademark authorization and confirmation cases, a people's court shall not treat the comparison of physical attributes of related goods as the sole criterion for determining whether goods are similar. Instead, it shall examine whether the functions, uses, production departments, sales channels, and consumer groups of the goods are the same or have significant relevance, and whether the coexistence of the two trademarks is likely to cause the relevant public to believe that the goods or services are provided by the same entity or that there is a specific connection between their providers, so as to comprehensively and reasonably determine whether the related goods are similar.

Notice of the Supreme People's Court Rejecting the Application for Retrial

(2011) Zhi Xing Zi No. 37

To: Hangzhou Woodpecker Shoes Co., Ltd.

Your company filed an application with this Court for retrial, dissatisfied with the administrative judgment (2010) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 743 (hereinafter referred to as the second-instance judgment) rendered by the Beijing High People's Court on December 2, 2010, in the case of the dispute over trademark administration with the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board) and Qihao (Group) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Qihao Company). This Court, after filing the case on March 29, 2011, formed a collegiate panel in accordance with the law to examine the case and organized a hearing for all parties on May 19, 2011. The examination has now been completed.

Your company's application for retrial states:

1. The second-instance judgment erred in finding that the Graphic Trademark No. 1609312 (hereinafter referred to as the disputed trademark) violated Article 28 of the Trademark Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Law), and that the factual findings and application of law were incorrect.

First, the premise for the application of Article 28 of the Trademark Law is that the goods are similar. However, the second-instance judgment did not determine whether the goods approved for use of the disputed trademark and the cited trademarks, namely "shoes" and "boots" and "clothing," "neckties," and "leather bags," are similar. Instead, it found that the disputed trademark and the cited trademarks constitute similar trademarks on the ground that the approved goods are all wearable items, so-called "related goods," and consequently determined that the disputed trademark violates Article 28 of the Trademark Law. This constitutes an error in the application of law.

Second, goods such as clothing and goods such as shoes differ significantly in functions, uses, production departments, sales channels, etc., and are not similar goods. This conclusion was already clearly reached in the judgment (2005) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 27. Moreover, in the Classification of Similar Goods and Services (hereinafter referred to as the Classification Table), goods such as shoes and boots and clothing are classified as non-similar goods. The Classification Table is the basis for trademark management by China's trademark authorities and a standard guideline for producers and service providers when applying for trademark registration. Its stability and uniformity should be maintained. Therefore, without sufficient evidence that goods such as shoes and boots and clothing have established a close connection commonly recognized by the relevant public in terms of raw materials, production, sales, consumption habits, etc., and without changes in international practice, the recognition of the non-similar relationship between these goods in the Classification Table should not be overridden.

Third, there are obvious differences in the composition details and design style between the graphic of the disputed trademark and that of the cited trademarks. The disputed trademark primarily uses a smearing, exaggerating, and coloring painting technique, which differs from the line-drawing technique mainly used in the cited trademarks.

Fourth, the disputed trademark has been used for many years and has become well known to consumers, and it will not cause confusion or misidentification among the relevant public.

In summary, the disputed trademark and the cited trademarks do not create a likelihood of confusion or misidentification among the relevant public, and do not constitute similar trademarks on similar goods. The second-instance judgment's factual findings and application of law on this issue are indeed erroneous.

2. The second-instance judgment's finding that the disputed trademark violated Article 41, Paragraph 1 of the Trademark Law is clearly erroneous in both factual findings and application of law.

First, the second-instance judgment's finding that the cited trademarks had some reputation before the application date of the disputed trademark lacks evidentiary support. During the trademark review procedure, Qihao Company failed to submit evidence of the domestic advertising or use of the cited trademarks before the application date of the disputed trademark. The second-instance judgment's conclusion that your company should have known about the cited trademarks is a pure subjective inference, without any factual or legal basis. Furthermore, the second-instance judgment's finding that the disputed trademark involves copying or imitating the cited trademarks lacks evidentiary support.

Second, during the trademark review procedure, Qihao Company did not request a review on the ground that the disputed trademark violated Article 41, Paragraph 1 of the Trademark Law, and the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board also did not conduct a review on this ground. The second-instance judgment directly applied this provision, exceeding the scope of review of the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board and depriving your company of the right to legitimate defense.

Third, according to the provisions of the Supreme People's Court's Opinions on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Administrative Cases Involving Trademark Authorization and Confirmation (hereinafter referred to as the Opinions), Article 41, Paragraph 1 of the Trademark Law applies only to absolute grounds, not to relative grounds. Therefore, even assuming that the copying or imitating conduct referred to in the second-instance judgment exists, it does not constitute "other improper means," and the second-instance judgment's application of law is erroneous.

3. Since the registration of the disputed trademark, your company has been committed to building the "Woodpecker" shoe brand, investing heavily in advertising and anti-counterfeiting and rights protection efforts. Through your company's vigorous promotion, Woodpecker shoes have become a well-known domestic brand. Pursuant to the policy spirit of Article 1 of the Opinions, for a trademark like the disputed trademark, which has been registered and used for up to ten years, has established a high market reputation, formed its own group of relevant consumers, and has become well-known, the people's court should respect the market reality that the relevant public has objectively distinguished the relevant trademarks, be cautious in canceling it, so as to promote brand cultivation and avoid waste of social resources. The second-instance judgment canceled the disputed trademark on specious grounds, clearly contradicting the relevant policy spirit.

In summary, your company requests the revocation of the second-instance judgment and the maintenance of the judgment of the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court (2009) Yi Zhong Xing Chu Zi No. 1068 (hereinafter referred to as the first-instance judgment) and the Decision on the Dispute of Graphic Trademark No. 1609312, Shang Ping Zi (2009) No. 2577 (hereinafter referred to as Decision No. 2577).

Qihao Company argues in its defense:

1. The second-instance court correctly applied Article 28 of the Trademark Law by finding that "shoes" and "clothing" constitute related goods and that the disputed trademark and the cited trademarks constitute similar trademarks.

2. The grounds for Qihao Company's cancellation application included that the copying of the cited trademark constituted unfair competition, so the second-instance court's application of Article 41, Paragraph 1 of the Trademark Law is not improper. Moreover, since the disputed trademark violates Article 28 of the Trademark Law, whether Article 41, Paragraph 1 applies does not affect the final outcome.

3. The evidence provided by your company is insufficient to prove the reputation of the disputed trademark. Your company operates on a very small scale and primarily relies on free-riding on famous brands, so protection should not be granted.

The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board states its opinion as follows:

1. The Classification Table is a professional normative document formed by China's trademark authorities, based on the International Classification of Goods and Services for the Purposes of the Registration of Marks provided by the World Intellectual Property Organization, summarizing China's long-term trademark examination practice and taking into account China's national conditions, to determine whether goods and services are similar. It has the characteristics of openness, consistency, and stability. The classification of similar goods in the table is itself based on a comprehensive consideration of factors such as the function, use, production department, sales channel, and target consumers of the goods. In the trademark confirmation procedure, consistency in the criteria for determining similar goods needs to be maintained. Admittedly, because of updates in goods and services items and changes in market trading conditions, the similarity relationship between similar goods and services is not static. However, amendments to the Classification Table should be made uniformly through a certain procedure and published to ensure the relative stability of the judgment criteria and the fairness and order of trademark examination, to avoid confusion for trademark applicants when applying for registration, and to ensure the stability of registered trademark rights. In this case, the goods designated for the disputed trademark, shoes and boots, and the goods approved for the cited trademarks, such as clothing, neckties, etc., have obvious differences in manufacturing materials, production processes, functions, uses, sales channels, etc., and do not constitute similar goods. Therefore, the disputed trademark and the cited trademarks do not constitute similar trademarks used on identical or similar goods.

2. During the administrative procedure, Qihao Company did not request a review on the ground that the disputed trademark violated Article 41, Paragraph 1 of the Trademark Law. The second-instance judgment directly applied this provision and canceled Decision No. 2577, exceeding the scope of trial of this case. Therefore, we request the revocation of the second-instance judgment and the maintenance of Decision No. 2577.

Upon examination, this Court finds that the disputed trademark in this case was applied for registration by your company on May 26, 2000, with the Trademark Office of the State Administration for Industry and Commerce of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Trademark Office), for use on goods in Class 25, Group 2507, namely shoes and boots, with the designated color being the entire woodpecker body in black and the lower part of the beak in green. The Trademark Office approved the registration of the trademark on August 7, 2001, with Registration No. 1609312.

Cited Trademark 1 is the "Bird Graphic + TUCANO" trademark applied for by Qihao Company on January 3, 1993, with the Trademark Office for registration on clothing goods in Class 25. The Trademark Office approved the registration on March 7, 1994, with Registration No. 680928. After renewal, the exclusive rights period extends to 2014.

Cited Trademark 2 is the "Bird Graphic" trademark applied for by Qihao Company on September 13, 1999, with the Trademark Office for registration on clothing goods in Class 25. The Trademark Office approved the registration on December 21, 2000, with Registration No. 1493162.

Cited Trademark 3 is the "Bird Graphic + TUCANO" trademark applied for by Qihao Company on October 21, 1999, with the Trademark Office for registration on goods such as neckties, scarves, and belts (for clothing) in Class 25, Groups 2501, 2509-2512. The Trademark Office approved the registration on March 21, 2001, with Registration No. 1541673.

Cited Trademark 4 is the "Bird Graphic" trademark applied for by Qihao Company on March 5, 1997, with the Trademark Office for registration on goods in Class 18, such as leather bags, travel bags, and briefcases. The Trademark Office approved the registration on April 21, 1998, with Registration No. 1168550.

On February 3, 2004, Qihao Company filed an application with the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board to cancel the registration of the disputed trademark. Qihao Company argued that it had registered the "Bird Graphic + TUCANO" and "Bird Graphic" trademarks for goods in Classes 25 and 18. Through use, these trademarks had become world-renowned clothing brands and had been judicially recognized as well-known trademarks. The disputed trademark constituted preemptive registration of another's well-known trademark, infringing Qihao Company's lawful rights and interests; the disputed trademark and the cited trademarks constituted similar trademarks used on similar goods, and also infringed Qihao Company's copyright. Therefore, Qihao Company requested the cancellation of the disputed trademark. During the review period, Qihao Company submitted evidence such as decisions from industry and commerce authorities in Anhui, Zhejiang, and Chengdu, etc., regarding penalties for infringement of the cited trademarks from 2001 to 2003.

During the review period, your company submitted evidence including a television advertising contract for "Woodpecker Shoes" signed in August 2001, a declaration published in Anhui Consumer News on November 15, 2002, regarding counterfeiting of the "Woodpecker" shoe trademark, decisions issued by local industry and commerce authorities in Zhejiang Province from 2001 to 2004 regarding infringement of "Woodpecker Shoes," reports from media such as Jianghuai Morning Post, Anhui Market News, and Fujian Economic Express from October to December 2002, regarding infringement of "Woodpecker Shoes," and Civil Judgment (2007) Zhou Min San Chu Zi No. 32 of the Xiangxi Tujia and Miao Autonomous Prefecture Intermediate People's Court of Hunan Province, along with a certificate of its entry into force, which confirmed that your company's Graphic Trademark No. 1609312 (i.e., the disputed trademark) and Trademark No. 1525486 "Woodpecker" were well-known trademarks in China.

The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board held in its review that the goods designated for the disputed trademark, shoes and boots, and the goods designated for the cited trademarks, such as clothing, neckties, and leather bags, belong to different scopes and fields, and consumers have different channels for obtaining these goods. In the Classification Table, they are not in the same similar group and are not similar goods. The disputed trademark and the cited trademarks do not constitute similar trademarks used on identical or similar goods. The evidence submitted by Qihao Company is insufficient to prove that the cited trademarks were well-known before the application date of the disputed trademark; therefore, the registration of the disputed trademark does not constitute the circumstance referred to in Article 13, Paragraph 2 of the Trademark Law. The "Bird Graphic" trademark of Qihao Company is a common woodpecker pattern, lacking strong distinctiveness, and the bird graphics of the disputed trademark and the cited trademarks have certain differences in composition details and design style. Therefore, there is insufficient reason to find that the registration of the disputed trademark constitutes infringement of another's copyright. Accordingly, on February 23, 2009, the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board issued Decision No. 2577, maintaining the registration of the disputed trademark.

Qihao Company, dissatisfied with Decision No. 2577, filed an administrative lawsuit with the Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court within the statutory period. The Beijing No. 1 Intermediate People's Court held in the first instance that the goods designated for the disputed trademark, shoes and boots, and the goods designated for the cited trademarks, such as clothing, neckties, and leather bags, are not similar goods. Use of the disputed trademark and the cited trademarks on non-similar goods would not cause ordinary consumers to confuse or misidentify the source of the goods. The evidence submitted by Qihao Company is insufficient to prove that the cited trademarks were well-known trademarks before the application date of the disputed trademark. The bird graphics in the disputed trademark and the cited trademarks differ in design technique and expression form, and the disputed trademark does not infringe the copyright of the bird graphic. Therefore, the first-instance court rendered a judgment on December 31, 2009, maintaining Decision No. 2577.

Qihao Company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Beijing High People's Court. Qihao Company supplemented the second-instance court with the following evidence: (1) a contract signed on May 1, 1996, between the company and Zhejiang Laiqu Lai Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Laiqu Lai Company), stipulating "the authorization to Laiqu Lai Company as the exclusive agent of the Woodpecker brand apparel in China, granting production rights and authentication rights for Woodpecker brand men's apparel, allowing self-production, and permitting use of the Woodpecker registered trademark on products such as T-shirts, sweaters, etc."; (2) a contract jointly signed by Laiqu Lai Company and Zhejiang Huameng Co., Ltd. in September 1996, for the formation of "Zhejiang Woodpecker Apparel Co., Ltd.," along with business license contents and procedures for the change of company name; (3) the program for the 1997 CCTV Spring Festival Gala, which included an advertising insert for Woodpecker (China) Apparel Co., Ltd.'s advertisement for its Woodpecker series of apparel, and brochures for Woodpecker apparel from the company; (4) your company's registration information and Qihao Company's goods using the Woodpecker graphic; (5) reports and comments from various media regarding the imitation and use of "Woodpecker"; (6) letters of investigation from industry and commerce authorities in recent years regarding infringement of Qihao Company's "Bird Graphic" and other trademarks. The second-instance court, finding that Qihao Company failed to state justifiable reasons for not submitting the above evidence during the review stage and the first-instance stage, did not accept the evidence.

The Beijing High People's Court held in the second instance that although Qihao Company claimed during the administrative and litigation proceedings that its "Bird Graphic," "Woodpecker" Chinese characters, and "Bird Graphic + TUCANO" trademarks had been judicially recognized as well-known trademarks in 2005, that recognition occurred after the application date of the disputed trademark and cannot prove that the above trademarks were well-known before the application date of the disputed trademark. However, the relevant evidence submitted by Qihao Company is sufficient to show that its cited trademarks had a certain degree of reputation in mainland China before the application date of the disputed trademark, through use and advertising. Since the "Bird Graphic" of the cited trademarks originates from the inherent figure of a woodpecker, and Qihao Company acquired the cited trademarks through assignment and is not the original designer, Qihao Company did not submit evidence proving its copyright in the "Bird Graphic" of the cited trademarks. The second-instance court thus agreed with the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board and the first-instance court on this matter. Although the "Woodpecker Graphic" of the disputed trademark and the "Bird Graphic" of the cited trademarks have slight differences in partial design, the overall shapes are essentially the same. Therefore, under isolated comparison, the overall appearances of the trademark identifiers are similar. Furthermore, although the goods designated for the disputed trademark and the cited trademarks are not in the same similar group in the Classification Table, they are all wearable items, and the goods and the enterprises producing them have a very strong correlation. Therefore, the goods for which use is approved should be considered related goods; their coexistence in the market is likely to cause consumers to confuse or misidentify the source of the goods. Thus, the disputed trademark and the cited trademarks constitute similar trademarks. Given that the cited trademarks of Qihao Company had some reputation before the application date of the disputed trademark, and that both companies are producers of apparel, shoes, and hats, with a strong correlation between the two enterprises, your company should have known about Qihao Company's cited trademarks. Because Qihao Company's cited trademark "Bird Graphic" was used earlier, and the design of the disputed trademark identifier is similar to the cited trademarks, there is copying and imitation of the cited trademarks, which falls under the circumstance of registration by improper means provided in Article 41, Paragraph 1 of the Trademark Law. Accordingly, the second-instance court found that Decision No. 2577 and the first-instance judgment's determination on the above facts does not comply with Articles 28 and 41, Paragraph 1 of the Trademark Law and should be revoked. Therefore, the second-instance court ruled to revoke the first-instance judgment and Decision No. 2577.

Additionally, it is established that, based on the evidence submitted by your company, your company not only registered the disputed trademark and other "Bird Graphic" trademarks for shoes, but also registered the "TUCANO" and "Woodpecker" trademarks in 2000 and 2001 respectively, and often uses the "Bird Graphic," "TUCANO," and "Woodpecker" together in use. Through business operations, your company's products and trademarks have gained a certain degree of reputation. The evidence submitted by Qihao Company proves that the cited trademarks had some reputation before the application date of the disputed trademark through authorized use and advertising in mainland China. Subsequently, the scale of use of the cited trademarks expanded further, and they now have high recognition.

Further examination revealed that when Qihao Company filed an application with the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board for revocation of the disputed trademark, it asserted that the disputed trademark was a copy and imitation of the bird pattern of the cited trademark, infringing its copyright, and also asserted that your company's use of "Zhuomu Niao" as a trade name would cause further confusion, constituting an act of unfair competition. However, it did not explicitly assert that the disputed trademark violated the provisions of Article 41(1) of the Trademark Law. When Qihao Company, dissatisfied with Ruling No. 2577, initiated the first-instance lawsuit, it also did not assert that the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board had omitted the review or raise any relevant objections regarding this issue.

Opinion of the Court:

I. Regarding the Application of Article 41(1) of the Trademark Law

First, trademark dispute proceedings are initiated upon request, and the grounds for dispute are generally limited to those asserted by the parties. The corresponding litigation is also limited to the review of the administrative adjudication, and generally no new grounds may be introduced to examine and determine the legality of trademark registration. From the facts found, when Qihao Company filed the application for revocation of the disputed trademark, it did not assert that the registration of the disputed trademark violated Article 41(1) of the Trademark Law. The Trademark Review and Adjudication Board did not conduct an examination on this issue, and Qihao Company also did not raise any objection in this regard when filing the first-instance lawsuit or the second-instance appeal. Under the circumstances where the applicant did not assert the claim and the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board did not conduct the review, the court of second instance directly determined that the disputed trademark constituted a copy or imitation of the cited trademark, and further determined that the disputed trademark fell under the circumstances of registration by improper means as stipulated in Article 41(1) of the Trademark Law, which lacks legal basis. Second, the "improper means" stipulated in Article 41(1) of the Trademark Law refer to means other than deceptive means that disrupt the order of trademark registration, harm the public interest, improperly occupy public resources, or seek illegitimate interests by other means. For situations that only harm specific civil rights and interests, the examination and determination shall be conducted pursuant to Article 41(2) and (3) of the Trademark Law and other corresponding provisions of the Trademark Law. In this case, even if, as the court of second instance determined, the disputed trademark copied or imitated the cited trademark, it only harmed the civil rights and interests of Qihao Company. It does not constitute an act of disrupting the order of trademark registration, harming the public interest, improperly occupying public resources, or seeking illegitimate interests by other means, and thus does not constitute "improper means" as stipulated in Article 41(1) of the Trademark Law. In summary, the determination by the court of second instance that the disputed trademark violated Article 41(1) of the Trademark Law was erroneous, and this Court hereby corrects it.

II. Regarding Whether the Disputed Trademark and the Cited Trademark Constitute Similar Trademarks on Similar Goods

According to the Trademark Law, if a trademark applied for registration is identical or similar to a trademark that has already been registered or preliminarily approved by another person for use on the same or similar goods, the Trademark Office shall reject the application and shall not publish the trademark. If the registrant of an earlier registered trademark believes that a later-filed trademark application is identical or similar to its registered trademark on the same or similar goods, it may, within five years from the date of approval of the registration of the later-filed trademark, apply to the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board for a ruling.

The main function of a trademark is to indicate the source of goods or services; therefore, a trademark must be associated with specific goods or services. The Trademark Law establishes the relationship of similarity between goods because trademarks are mainly registered, managed, and protected according to the class of goods. In the process of determining trademark authorization, confirmation, and infringement, the determination of whether related goods are similar for the purposes of trademark law does not involve a comparison of the physical attributes of the goods, but rather mainly considers whether the trademarks can coexist or determines the scope of trademark protection. Avoiding confusion as to source is a fundamental principle to adhere to when determining the similarity of goods. Therefore, when a people's court hears a case concerning trademark authorization and confirmation, in examining and determining whether related goods are similar, it shall consider whether the functions, uses, production departments, sales channels, and consumer groups of the goods are the same or have a significant correlation, and whether the coexistence of the two trademarks is likely to cause the relevant public to believe that the goods or services are provided by the same entity, or that there is a specific connection between their providers.

In this case, the goods designated for use with the disputed trademark are shoes and boots, while the goods for which the cited trademark is approved for use include clothing, etc. Although there are some differences in specific raw materials, uses, etc., between the two, their consumer groups are the same. Moreover, in the current commercial environment, it is common for a single manufacturer to produce both clothing and footwear, and for clothing and footwear to be sold through the same channels, such as in the same specialty store or counter. At the same time, although the "bird pattern" in the disputed trademark and the cited trademark have slight differences in detail, their basic forms are the same. Furthermore, according to the facts found, the cited trademark has a relatively high degree of recognition through use. Under such circumstances, if the two trademarks coexist on clothing and footwear, it is likely to cause the relevant public to believe that the two goods are provided by the same entity, or that there is a specific connection between their providers. Therefore, the disputed trademark and the cited trademark constitute similar trademarks on similar goods. Your company's assertion that the disputed trademark and the cited trademark are not similar and that the goods designated for use are not similar goods cannot be sustained.

The Classification Table is a normative document formulated by China's trademark authorities based on the International Classification of Goods and Services for the Purposes of the Registration of Marks provided by the World Intellectual Property Organization, summarizing China's long-term trademark examination practice and taking into account China's national conditions, for determining the similarity of goods and services. The classification of similar goods in this table is determined on the basis of comprehensively considering factors such as the function, use, production department, sales channel, and target consumers of the goods. Therefore, the Classification Table can serve as a reference for determining similar goods or services. Particularly in trademark registration application examination, which emphasizes objectivity, consistency, and ease of operation, it is consistent with the inherent laws of trademark registration examination for the trademark administrative authorities to use the Classification Table as the standard for dividing similar goods and to conduct trademark registration and management based on this table, in order to ensure uniformity and efficiency in law enforcement. However, the items of goods and services and market transaction conditions are constantly changing, and the similarity relationship between similar goods and services is not static. Furthermore, trademark oppositions and disputes are institutional arrangements distinct from trademark registration application examination, bearing different institutional functions and value orientations. They more often involve the protection of specific civil rights and interests, emphasize case-specificity and actual circumstances, and especially in cases that enter litigation, emphasize judicial relief on a case-by-case basis. In these stages, if maintaining consistency and stability is prioritized without considering actual circumstances and case-specific factors, it would deviate from the purpose and function of the institutional design. Therefore, when determining the similarity of goods in trademark oppositions, disputes, subsequent litigation, and infringement lawsuits, the Classification Table should not be used mechanically or simply as the sole basis or standard; instead, more practical factors should be considered, and the determination should be made in light of the specific circumstances of the case. The revision of the Classification Table has its own rules and procedures, cannot address lag, and cannot account for case-specific circumstances. Relying on the revision of the Classification Table to accurately determine the similarity of goods in individual cases is unrealistic and illogical. On the contrary, case-specific determinations and breakthroughs can promptly reflect changes in the relationship between goods and, when necessary, can also promote revisions to the Classification Table. Therefore, the view that revisions to the Classification Table must be uniformly made through a certain procedure and published, and otherwise cannot be deviated from, cannot be sustained. In fact, the Trademark Review and Adjudication Board has, in some review cases, already rendered rulings consistent with the actual circumstances, departing from the classification of similar goods in the Classification Table. Therefore, your company's contention that shoes and clothing are classified as non-similar goods in the Classification Table and should not be deviated from lacks legal basis, and this Court does not support it.

It must be emphasized that because the determination of similarity of goods considers case-specific circumstances, the similarity or non-similarity of related goods is not absolute or immutable; different conclusions may be reached based on different case scenarios. Therefore, the determination in the judgment of (2005) Gao Xing Zhong Zi No. 27 that clothing and footwear are not similar goods does not mean that they necessarily do not constitute similar goods under specific case circumstances. The determination in this case is not contradictory to that. At the same time, because the determination of the similarity of goods in a specific case considers case-specific circumstances and is case-specific, such a case-specific determination does not imply a change in the similarity relationship of goods in trademark registration management, nor does it necessarily affect the determination and classification of the similarity of goods in the Classification Table. A trademark applicant may still apply for registration based on the Classification Table. Similarly, a case-specific determination generally will not affect the stability of the right in a registered trademark.

Furthermore, "related goods" often refer to goods that are classified as non-similar in the Classification Table but actually have a strong correlation, and the coexistence of related trademarks is likely to cause confusion or misunderstanding. For such goods, they still need to be examined and determined within the framework of similar goods. As long as it is likely to cause the relevant public to believe that the goods or services are provided by the same entity, or that there is a specific connection between their providers, they legally constitute similar goods. In this case, the second-instance judgment determined that clothing and footwear are related goods, and further determined that the disputed trademark violated the provisions of Article 28 of the Trademark Law. This expression may easily lead to a misunderstanding that another classification of goods relationship has been created outside of similar goods. Therefore, this Court hereby corrects this.

III. Regarding the Relationship Between Actual Use and Whether a Trademark Should Be Cancelled

The true value of a trademark originates from actual use. Protecting the market reputation established through actual use is an important legislative spirit of the Trademark Law. Therefore, actual use is one of the important factors to consider when determining whether a trademark should be cancelled in trademark authorization and confirmation cases. For trademarks that have been used for a long time, have established a high market reputation, and have formed a relevant consumer group, the legislative spirit of the Trademark Law in coordinating the protection of prior business mark rights and the maintenance of market order should be accurately grasped. Full respect should be given to the market reality where the relevant public has objectively distinguished the relevant business marks, and emphasis should be placed on maintaining the market order that has been formed and stabilized. However, the overall principle of trademark authorization and confirmation procedures remains to curb free-riding and preemptive registration, protect prior trademarks of others, and eliminate as much as possible the possibility of confusion of business marks. In this case, based on the evidence submitted by your company, it can be seen that in addition to registering the disputed trademark and other series of "bird pattern" trademarks similar to Qihao Company's cited trademark, your company also registered trademarks such as "TUCANO" and "Zhuomu Niao" on footwear, and in actual business operations, often uses the "bird pattern" together with "TUCANO" and "Zhuomu Niao". Notably, "TUCANO" is a component of cited trademark No. 1, and "Zhuomu Niao" happens to be a trademark that Qihao Company had previously registered and actually used on goods such as clothing, and which has a certain degree of recognition. These circumstances indicate that your company has had the subjective intent to free-ride and imitate, from trademark registration to actual use. Although through your company's operations and actual use of the disputed trademark, your company's products and trademarks have also gained high recognition, because both your company and Qihao Company use similar "bird patterns" and the same trademarks such as "TUCANO" and "Zhuomu Niao" in their business activities, it is obvious that for the relevant public who do not know the details, they would believe that the providers are the same entity or have a specific connection, which is likely to cause source confusion. Therefore, in this case, a market reality where the relevant business marks have been objectively distinguished has not actually been formed. At the same time, although the holder of the cited trademark, Qihao Company, was also somewhat negligent in not promptly and actively applying for trademark registration on footwear when the Classification Table classified clothing and footwear as non-similar goods, thereby contributing to the current conflict, nevertheless, considering the basic principle of curbing free-riding and avoiding confusion, as well as your company's subjective intent and the objective reality of likely confusion and misunderstanding, and additionally, since your company owns other trademarks that are actually used besides the disputed trademark, cancelling the registration of the disputed trademark will not have a substantial impact on your company's operations. Your company can continue the goodwill built up over many years of operation through appropriate means and take this opportunity to create its own brand, thereby trying to eliminate the possibility of confusion with Qihao Company's business marks. Therefore, this Court holds that the conclusion of the second-instance judgment to revoke the disputed trademark is correct and should be affirmed. Your company's contention that the disputed trademark has been extensively used and should not be revoked is not supported by this Court.

In summary, this Court holds that although the second-instance judgment had some improper aspects regarding the application of the law, its conclusion is correct. Your company's application for retrial does not meet the retrial conditions stipulated in Article 63(2) of the Administrative Litigation Law of the PRC and Article 72 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Litigation Law of the PRC. Pursuant to Article 74 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues concerning the Implementation of the Administrative Litigation Law of the PRC, the application is hereby dismissed.

We hereby notify you.

July 12, 2011
